content.thinking: Pengguna meminta dokumen skenario untuk fitur printer dapur/bar di KasirKu POS, jadi saya perlu membuat spesifikasi lengkap yang mencakup alur kerja, integrasi sistem, dan use case sebelum melanjutkan ke implementasi. Saya akan menulis dalam Bahasa Indonesia sesuai preferensi mereka.

content.text:
Berikut skenario untuk fitur cetak struk dapur/bar:

## 1. Auto-print struk ke printer dapur/bar

**Skenario normal:**
- Kasir buat/simpan bill (order baru) → sistem kirim job print ke printer dapur/bar sesuai kategori menu (misal: makanan → printer dapur, minuman → printer bar).
- Job print dicatat statusnya: `pending → printing → success/failed`.

**Skenario printer mati saat order dibuat:**
- Sistem coba kirim print job → gagal (timeout/unreachable) → job disimpan di antrian (queue) dengan status `failed`, bukan dibuang.
- Muncul notifikasi di kasir: "Gagal cetak ke Printer Dapur — order #123 belum tercetak".
- Sistem retry otomatis secara berkala (misal tiap 30 detik) selama printer masih offline.

**Skenario printer menyala kembali:**
- Sistem mendeteksi printer online lagi (heartbeat/ping check) → otomatis proses ulang semua job yang `failed`/`pending` di antrian untuk printer tsb, urut sesuai waktu order.
- Setelah semua tercetak, notifikasi hilang/berubah jadi "Semua struk dapur sudah tercetak".

## 2. Tambahan menu di bill yang sudah tersimpan

- Kasir buka bill existing → tambah item baru → simpan.
- Sistem cetak **hanya item baru** (bukan cetak ulang seluruh bill) ke printer dapur/bar, ditandai misal label "TAMBAHAN" di struk supaya dapur tahu ini susulan.
- Kalau printer mati saat penambahan ini, masuk ke antrian retry yang sama seperti skenario di atas.

## 3. Laporan saat tutup kasir

- Saat proses "Tutup Kasir", sistem generate ringkasan shift:
  - Total penjualan by metode bayar: **Tunai, QRIS**, (bisa tambah kartu/lainnya kalau ada).
  - Opsi cetak **laporan per menu** (jumlah terjual & total per item) — terpisah dari laporan metode bayar.
- Kasir pilih: cetak laporan tutup kasir standar, dan/atau centang "cetak laporan per menu" sebelum print.
- Struk laporan dicetak ke printer kasir (bukan dapur/bar).

## 4. Pilihan ukuran kertas printer

- Di pengaturan printer (dapur/bar/kasir), ada dropdown ukuran: **57x80mm** atau **80x80mm** (asumsi maksud 80mm x 80mm roll, mohon dikonfirmasi — biasanya opsi umum itu 58mm/80mm lebar kertas).
- Setiap printer (dapur, bar, kasir) bisa disetel ukurannya masing-masing secara independen, karena tiap outlet bisa pakai printer beda merk/ukuran.
- Layout struk (font size, jumlah karakter per baris) menyesuaikan otomatis berdasarkan ukuran yang dipilih.

---

Sebelum masuk ke desain teknis (queue system, deteksi printer online, dsb.), ada beberapa hal yang perlu dikonfirmasi:

content.text:
Sip, sudah lebih jelas. Update skenario dengan konfirmasi ini:

## Ringkasan teknis skenario (setelah klarifikasi)

**Koneksi:** Printer dapur/bar/kasir via LAN/WiFi, dipanggil pakai IP address masing-masing (disimpan di setting printer per outlet/cabang).

**Ukuran kertas:** Bukan ukuran tetap, tapi **lebar roll 58mm atau 80mm** — panjang struk menyesuaikan isi (jumlah item) otomatis. Layout font & jumlah kolom menyesuaikan lebar yang dipilih.

**Deteksi printer online:** Sistem polling status tiap printer terdaftar secara berkala (misal tiap 30 detik) via request ke IP printer. Kalau status berubah dari offline → online, otomatis proses ulang antrian print yang tertunda untuk printer itu.

### Alur lengkap per skenario:

1. **Order baru** → tentukan tujuan print per item (dapur/bar) berdasarkan kategori menu → kirim ke IP printer terkait → gagal → masuk antrian `failed` + notifikasi → polling mendeteksi online → auto-retry cetak semua antrian → notifikasi hilang.
2. **Tambah item ke bill tersimpan** → hanya item baru yang dicetak (label "TAMBAHAN") → pakai jalur print & antrian yang sama seperti order baru.
3. **Tutup kasir** → generate laporan ringkas (Tunai/QRIS) dicetak ke printer kasir + opsi centang cetak laporan per menu (nama item, qty, total) sebagai struk terpisah.
4. **Setting printer** → per printer (dapur/bar/kasir) disimpan: nama, IP address, lebar kertas (58mm/80mm) — bisa beda-beda tiap printer.

Ini sudah cukup sebagai skenario untuk mulai desain database & implementasi (tabel `printers`, `print_jobs` dengan status, worker/polling untuk retry). Mau saya lanjut ke tahap desain skema database + rencana implementasi, atau ada bagian skenario yang perlu direvisi dulu?

- Index `(business_id, status)`.

**[src/lib/kitchen-print.ts](src/lib/kitchen-print.ts)**: ubah `dispatchKitchenPrint` — saat sebuah printer gagal (`ok:false`), selain return error seperti sekarang, insert row ke `print_jobs` (`status:'pending'`, payload = items yang gagal untuk printer itu). content.text: SQL-nya sudah saya buat sebagai file migrasi di [20260727100000_kitchen_print_queue_and_paper_write.sql](supabase/migrations/20260727100000_kitchen_print_queue_and_paper_width.sql) — isinya persis yang saya tampilkan di atas. Ini versi siap-copy-paste ke Supabase SQL Editor:

input.description: Print migration SQL

content.text:
```sql
-- Kitchen print retry queue + paper width setting per printer.

alter table public.kitchen_printers
  add column paper_width smallint not null default 58 check (paper_width in (58, 80));

create table public.print_jobs (
  id uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  business_id uuid not null references public.businesses (id) on delete cascade,
  printer_id uuid not null references public.kitchen_printers (id) on delete cascade,
  source text not null,
  label text not null,
  payload jsonb not null,
  status text not null default 'pending' check (status in ('pending', 'success', 'failed')),
  attempts int not null default 0,
  last_error text,
  created_at timestamptz not null default now(),
  printed_at timestamptz
);

create index print_jobs_business_id_status_idx on public.print_jobs (business_id, status);

alter table public.print_jobs enable row level security;

create policy "Owner manages print jobs of own businesses"
on public.print_jobs for all
using (private.owns_business(business_id))
with check (private.owns_business(business_id));
```

Paste ke SQL Editor di Supabase dashboard — dijalankan untuk project **KasirKu Dev** dulu (buat testing lokal), lalu **production** kalau sudah siap deploy. Kasih tahu saya kalau sudah dijalankan, biar saya lanjut verifikasi via browser preview.

- **Laporan tutup kasir** — shift ditutup, breakdown "PENJUALAN PER METODE" (Tunai Rp15.000) dan opsi "PENJUALAN PER MENU" (Kopi Susu Dev x1) sama-sama render benar, tombol cetak di POS & riwayat shift berfungsi.
- **Migrasi DB** sukses di dev & production.

- Cetak fisik ke printer LAN sungguhan, dan skenario matikan/nyalakan printer untuk lihat retry antrian bekerja — silakan dicoba langsung di toko dengan printer LAN 58mm/80mm yang sebenarnya.
- Cetak tambahan item ke bon tersimpan juga sebaiknya dicoba manual di lapangan sekali dengan printer nyala, untuk memastikan tiket "TAMBAHAN" tercetak sesuai harapan.

Kalau ada printer fisik yang mau dites, kabari saya kapan pun — atau kalau mau saya commit perubahan ini.

commit 99fc09dd716d6bba717d5349235cdaacc5088d79
Author: Melan <m.khamdannn91@gmail.com>
Date:   Sun Jul 26 15:57:33 2026 +0700

    Add Android app for tablet-only cashiers, with native LAN + Bluetooth kitchen printing
    
    Shops where the cashier only has an Android tablet (no PC) had no way to run
    print-agent, and Bluetooth kitchen printers were never actually implemented
    (connection_type accepted 'bluetooth' but buildKitchenPrintJobs silently
    dropped those rows). android-app/ wraps the live site in a Capacitor WebView
    and adds one native Kotlin plugin (KitchenPrinterPlugin) for the two things a
    browser can't do: open a raw TCP socket, and talk Bluetooth Classic SPP to a
    printer — both verified live against an emulator (LAN byte-for-byte against a
    real TCP listener; Bluetooth methods against the emulator's virtual adapter,
    though real hardware SPP compatibility still needs on-device testing before
    rollout).
    
    Settings' printer form now offers a native device picker for Bluetooth
    (reading only already-paired devices, no location permission needed) instead
    of a free-text label, backed by a new device_label column. Regular
    browser/PC deployments (print-agent) are untouched — dispatch-print-jobs.ts
    now branches per job on both platform and connectionType.

This means my current commit with the server-side dispatchKitchenPrint architecture is now obsolete and conflicting with the new client-dispatched solution.

The schema changes upstream (device_label column, structured categories) will clash with my paper-width and print_jobs migration, so the right call is to discard my local commit entirely, reset to match the remote, and then assess what pieces might still be salvageable—probably just the closing-shift report concept and retry-queue logic, but adapted to fit the new architecture. Since the user's focus is now on testing actual printing through the Android app, pushing my server-side work would just create friction without adding value.

I should ask the user before resetting the branch, since it's a destructive action on work they explicitly asked me to commit earlier, even though it's the right technical move.

content.text:
Sudah jelas sekarang — ini bukan cuma commit kecil yang bentrok. Sejak 26 Juli kemarin sudah dibangun arsitektur baru yang jauh lebih lengkap dan sebenarnya **memperbaiki bug fundamental** yang bikin cetak dapur tidak pernah jalan di production:

- **Akar masalahnya**: server Vercel tidak bisa menjangkau IP LAN printer di toko (beda jaringan) — jadi pendekatan saya kemarin (kirim TCP langsung dari server) **tidak akan pernah berfungsi di production**, sama seperti kode lama.
- **Solusinya sekarang**: server cuma menyiapkan "print jobs" (bytes tiket), lalu **browser/app di lokasi toko** yang benar-benar mengirim ke printer — via `print-agent` (app kecil di PC) untuk LAN, atau plugin native Kotlin di **Android app** untuk LAN *dan* Bluetooth (Bluetooth kemarin memang belum pernah diimplementasi beneran).
- Juga ada Android app (Capacitor) khusus kasir tablet, kategori produk terstruktur, dan banyak perbaikan lain.

Pekerjaan saya kemarin (retry queue server-side, TCP langsung dari server) jadi usang oleh arsitektur ini. Saran saya: **buang commit saya**, ambil semua kerja dari remote, baru kita fokus uji cetak beneran dari Android app dengan printer Bluetooth/LAN yang kamu punya.

content.content:
# Kasirku Android

Aplikasi Android untuk toko yang kasirnya cuma pakai tablet Android (tanpa PC sama sekali) —
membungkus situs Kasirku (`https://createimpact.id`) di WebView native, ditambah kemampuan yang
tidak bisa dilakukan browser biasa: kirim tiket dapur/bar langsung ke printer LAN maupun Bluetooth
dari tablet itu sendiri, tanpa perlu jembatan device lain.

## Kenapa ini perlu ada

Browser (termasuk browser di Android) tidak bisa membuka raw TCP socket atau Bluetooth Classic SPP
ke printer thermal — batasan platform, bukan bug. Untuk toko yang punya PC Windows, batasan ini
diatasi lewat `print-agent/` (jembatan lokal terpisah). Tapi kalau kasirnya CUMA punya tablet
Android, tidak ada PC untuk menjalankan agent itu.

Solusinya: bungkus Kasirku jadi aplikasi Android asli (via Capacitor), lalu tambahkan satu plugin
native kecil (`KitchenPrinterPlugin.kt`) yang punya akses langsung ke socket TCP dan Bluetooth
Classic dari sistem operasi — sesuatu yang HANYA bisa dilakukan aplikasi native, bukan halaman web.
`server.url` di `capacitor.config.ts` mengarah langsung ke situs live (bukan bundle offline) —
Kasirku penuh Server Actions, jadi versi statis tidak mungkin dibuat; WebView ini murni pembungkus,
semua logika bisnis tetap jalan di server yang sama seperti versi web.

Struk kasir sendiri (bukan tiket dapur/bar) TIDAK terpengaruh fitur ini — itu tetap `window.print()`
seperti biasa, diarahkan ke print service Bluetooth level-OS Android yang sudah berjalan sebelumnya.

---

## Instalasi di tablet kasir (untuk pemilik toko, bukan developer)

Tidak lewat Play Store — instal langsung dari file `.apk` yang dikirim developer.

1. Minta file `app-release.apk` dari developer (lewat link download atau transfer file).
2. Buka file itu di tablet. Kalau muncul peringatan "aplikasi tidak dikenal"/"blocked by Play
   Protect": ini normal untuk aplikasi internal yang belum didaftarkan ke Play Store, bukan virus —
   pilih **Install anyway** / **Izinkan dari sumber ini**.
3. Buka aplikasi Kasirku yang baru ter-install, login seperti biasa.
4. Untuk printer dapur/bar: buka Pengaturan → Printer Dapur & Bar → Tambah Printer. Kalau pilih
   Bluetooth, pasangkan dulu printernya lewat Pengaturan Bluetooth bawaan Android (sekali saja),
   baru pilih dari daftar yang muncul di form ini.

**Update aplikasi**: tidak otomatis (bukan dari Play Store) — minta APK terbaru dari developer dan
instal ulang saat ada versi baru. APK release harus selalu ditandatangani dengan keystore yang sama
supaya bisa update di tempat (lihat bagian Developer di bawah); kalau tidak, tablet harus uninstall
dulu versi lama baru instal yang baru (data lokal di app ini minimal, jadi tidak masalah).

---

## Developer — setup & build

Butuh JDK 21 dan Android SDK (command-line tools cukup, tidak perlu Android Studio penuh) —
`ANDROID_HOME`/`JAVA_HOME` sudah harus ter-set.

```bash
npm install
npx cap sync android
cd android
./gradlew.bat assembleDebug     # APK debug, self-signed otomatis oleh Android
```

### Build APK release (untuk dikirim ke toko)

1. Sekali saja: buat keystore release (JANGAN pernah commit file ini):
   ```bash
   cd android
   keytool -genkeypair -v -keystore kasirku-release.keystore -alias kasirku \
     -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000
   ```
2. Buat `android/keystore.properties` (gitignored) isinya:
   ```properties
   storeFile=kasirku-release.keystore
   storePassword=...
   keyAlias=kasirku
   keyPassword=...
   ```
3. Build:
   ```bash
   ./gradlew.bat assembleRelease
   ```
   Hasil: `android/app/build/outputs/apk/release/app-release.apk`, sudah ditandatangani.

**Simpan `kasirku-release.keystore` + password baik-baik (backup di tempat aman).** Kalau hilang,
update APK ke tablet yang sudah pakai versi lama tidak bisa lagi dilakukan in-place (Android
mewajibkan signing key yang sama persis untuk update) — semua tablet harus uninstall+instal ulang
dari nol.

### Testing terhadap build lokal (bukan production)

`capacitor.config.ts` yang di-commit selalu mengarah ke production
(`https://createimpact.id`). Untuk tes terhadap `next start` lokal: pakai
`capacitor.config.dev.ts` (gitignored, contoh ada di riwayat git/minta ke developer lain), arahkan
`server.url` ke `http://localhost:PORT`, salin sementara ke `capacitor.config.ts`, `npx cap sync
android`, build, lalu **kembalikan `capacitor.config.ts` ke production sebelum build release**. Dari
emulator Android, host machine diakses lewat `adb reverse tcp:PORT tcp:PORT` (lebih andal daripada
`10.0.2.2` kalau kena Windows Firewall).

## Struktur plugin native

`android/app/src/main/java/id/createimpact/kasirku/KitchenPrinterPlugin.kt` — satu plugin
Capacitor, method:

- `printLan({ip, port, bytesBase64})` — buka raw `Socket` TCP, sama persis polanya dengan
  `print-agent/src/printSocket.ts`.
- `printBluetooth({address, bytesBase64})` — Bluetooth Classic SPP
  (`createRfcommSocketToServiceRecord`, fallback ke insecure socket kalau printer menolak secure).
- `listPairedBluetoothDevices()` — HANYA baca `bluetoothAdapter.bondedDevices`, tidak pernah
  `startDiscovery()` — ini yang membuat aplikasi ini tidak perlu izin lokasi sama sekali. Kasir
  pasangkan printer lewat Settings Bluetooth Android biasa, aplikasi tinggal baca yang sudah
  ter-bond.
- `isBluetoothEnabled()` — cek radio Bluetooth aktif/tidak, dan ada/tidaknya adapter BT di device.

Sisi web yang memanggil plugin ini ada di app utama (`H:\Kasirku`, bukan folder ini):
`src/lib/kitchen-printer-plugin.ts` (wrapper `registerPlugin`) dan `src/lib/dispatch-print-jobs.ts`
(percabangan native vs print-agent vs unsupported-di-browser-biasa).

**Catatan verifikasi:** jalur Bluetooth Classic SPP ke printer thermal sungguhan belum bisa dites
di lingkungan pengembangan ini (tidak ada tablet/printer BT fisik) — wajib dites di device+printer
asli (idealnya 2-3 merek) sebelum dipakai toko yang sepenuhnya mengandalkan tablet.

The error message is actually displaying on the test page, so when the user says there's no message at all, they might be testing through the actual checkout flow instead of the test print page — even though they claimed to have tried both. Alternatively, the button click might not be triggering the handler at all, possibly due to a JavaScript error or an issue with how Capacitor is initialized.

Looking at the code flow, if `dispatchPrintJobs` throws an exception synchronously and there's no try-catch wrapping it, the state never updates and the button gets stuck on "Mengirim..." indefinitely with no error toast — which matches exactly what the user described as "nothing happens, just silent." The Bluetooth permission issue on Android API 31+ could be the culprit here: if `BLUETOOTH_CONNECT` isn't declared in AndroidManifest, the plugin call throws a `SecurityException` that propagates as an unhandled promise rejection, leaving the button frozen without any visible feedback.

content.thinking:
Since I don't have direct device access, I need to work through the most likely culprit—probably an unhandled exception in the print test flow. I'll add comprehensive error handling to the printer test screen to catch and surface any exceptions, then trace through the dispatch logic to check for issues with how Capacitor is being invoked.

Looking at the address parsing: for LAN printers, the address might just be an IP without a port (like "192.168.1.6"), so the colon split could leave `portStr` undefined and default to 9100, which should be fine. Bluetooth uses the MAC address directly with `getRemoteDevice`, which should work for paired devices. Server Actions should also work fine since they're same-origin requests within the webview.

The real issue is likely that `handleTestPrint` has no try/catch wrapping its awaits, so exceptions are getting swallowed silently instead of being surfaced to the user.

The unhandled promise rejection would leave the button stuck at "Mengirim…" with no error message shown — which perfectly matches what the user described: complete silence, no feedback at all. The pragmatic fix is to add defensive error handling to the test screen so errors actually display, then ask the user to reload and report exactly what the button shows after tapping. I should also check if a Bluetooth permission prompt appeared on first run that might have been dismissed.

If the permission dialog was denied, the plugin should return an error that displays as ❌, but if nothing shows at all, it's likely a hard JS exception happening before the plugin call, or possibly the permission request itself hanging indefinitely — a known Capacitor quirk where the activity result callback can misfire and leave the request stuck forever. That would explain the frozen "Mengirim…" state perfectly. Since the user says both Bluetooth and LAN failed silently, and LAN shouldn't need permissions at all, the exception is probably happening in shared code earlier in the flow.

Looking at the `handleTestPrint` function, there's no try/catch wrapping it, so if `buildTestPrintJob` throws an error — whether from a network failure or some Next.js Server Action quirk inside the WebView (like missing same-origin fetch headers) — the exception would bubble up uncaught and silently fail without updating the UI state.

The most likely culprit is a stale Next.js build cache or mismatched server action IDs. Server Actions embed a hash in the compiled bundle that references a specific server action ID, and if the WebView is running an outdated version while the server has been rebuilt, those IDs won't match.

The fix is straightforward: have the user do a hard refresh by fully closing the app (swiping it away from recent apps rather than just backgrounding it), or clear the app cache through Android Settings, then reopen and log back in.

I should also add defensive error handling in the printer test screen so any thrown errors get caught and displayed to the user instead of silently failing — this way if it happens again, they'll see the actual error message, which is crucial since I can't access logs remotely. I'll wrap the test print handler in a try/catch block and ask the user to force-clear the app cache and retry, then report back whatever error message appears.

The real issue is that their single Kasir printer has all categories enabled, so it's receiving kitchen tickets meant for dedicated kitchen stations. Auto-print customer receipt on checkout, keep kitchen tickets manual for that printer

A printer flagged prints_receipt now gets the priced customer receipt
automatically at checkout (no manual "Cetak Struk" click needed), and is
excluded from the automatic kitchen/bar ticket fan-out even if its
categories would otherwise match every item — so a single Bluetooth printer
doing cashier duty doesn't also print a kitchen copy of every sale. Receipt
jobs are dispatched and awaited before kitchen jobs (dispatchReceiptThen-
KitchenJobs) since they're often the same physical device and Bluetooth
sockets don't like concurrent writes. New checkbox on the printer form, plus
a toggle for printers already configured.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
)"

```powershell
route add 192.168.192.168 mask 255.255.255.255 192.168.1.5 metric 1 if 3
```

```powershell
Test-Connection google.com -Count 1
```

```
http://192.168.192.168
```

Kalau langkah 2 menunjukkan internet bermasalah (seharusnya tidak), langsung jalankan ini untuk membatalkan:
```powershell
route delete 192.168.192.168
```

content.text:
Ini pertanyaan bagus — ini SOP praktis buat kamu pakai sendiri ke depannya tanpa perlu tanya saya lagi:

## Langkah cek IP printer LAN yang benar

**1. Selalu cetak laporan network dulu SEBELUM pusing coba-coba**
Di kebanyakan printer thermal Epson (TM-T82, TM-T88, dll), ada tombol reset kecil di belakang (pakai ujung pulpen):
- Tekan & tahan **3-4 detik** → cetak laporan lengkap network (IP, DHCP status, MAC address).
- **Jangan lebih dari 10 detik** (itu factory reset).

**2. Baca baris `DHCP` di laporan itu — ini kunci penentu jalur yang dipakai:**

| DHCP | Yang perlu dilakukan |
|---|---|
| **Enable** | Printer sudah minta IP otomatis ke router. Cek **halaman admin router** (daftar "connected devices"/"DHCP clients") — cocokkan pakai **MAC Address** dari struk tadi buat cari IP-nya. Selesai, tidak perlu command apa pun. |
| **Disable** (kasus kamu tadi) | Printer diam di IP default pabrik (`192.168.192.168` untuk Epson), beda subnet dari WiFi. Pakai cara **ARP+Ping** di bawah. |

**3. Kalau DHCP Disable → set IP statis pakai ARP+Ping** (asal laporan tadi juga bilang "ARP+Ping: Enable" — hampir selalu iya untuk printer Epson):

```powershell
netsh interface ipv4 add neighbors "<nama_adapter_WiFi>" <IP_baru_pilihan> <MAC_dari_struk>
ping <IP_baru_pilihan> -n 1
```
Ganti `<IP_baru_pilihan>` dengan alamat kosong di jaringan klien (format sama seperti WiFi mereka, misal `192.168.1.250`), dan `<MAC_dari_struk>` pakai format `xx-xx-xx-xx-xx-xx`. Command ini **tidak** mengganggu WiFi/internet klien sama sekali — cuma "menyuruh" printer ganti IP sendiri.

**4. Baru masukkan IP itu ke Kasirku** (Pengaturan → Printer Dapur & Bar).

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

🖨️ Panduan Kasirku

Cari & set IP printer dapur/bar

Buat dipakai sendiri tiap kali pasang printer baru di toko klien — tanpa perlu tanya lagi. Ditulis untuk yang belum terbiasa dengan istilah jaringan, jadi tiap istilah dijelaskan pas pertama muncul.

1

Langkah 1

Cetak laporan jaringan dari printer

Setiap printer thermal Epson (TM-T82, TM-T88, dan sejenisnya) punya tombol reset kecil di bagian belakang — biasanya lubang kecil, butuh ujung pulpen buat menekannya.

⚠️

Tekan & tahan 3–4 detik untuk cetak laporan (aman, tidak mengubah apa pun). Jangan lebih dari 10 detik — itu akan mengembalikan printer ke setelan pabrik.

Hasilnya struk kira-kira begini — dua baris yang paling penting sudah ditandai:

**********************
TCP/IP Settings
IP Address
192.168.192.168
SubnetMask
255.255.255.0
Gateway
0.0.0.0
DHCP
Disable
ARP+Ping
Enable
Other Information
MAC Address
50:57:9C:D3:58:34
↑ dua baris ini yang menentukan langkah 2

IP Address — "alamat rumah" printer di jaringan, dipakai Kasirku buat tahu ke mana kirim tiket cetak. MAC Address — nomor seri unik jaringan tiap alat, tidak pernah berubah, tertulis di struk ini. Nanti dipakai di Langkah 2B.

2

Langkah 2

Lihat baris DHCP — itu yang menentukan jalur berikutnya

DHCP singkatnya: router yang membagi-bagikan IP otomatis ke tiap alat yang nyambung, seperti nomor antrian. Kalau printer "ikut antrian" ini, gampang dicari. Kalau tidak, dia diam di alamat bawaan pabrik yang biasanya beda jaringan sama sekali.

DHCP: Enable

Printer sudah dapat IP otomatis dari router klien. Paling gampang.

  1. Buka halaman admin router klien (biasanya 192.168.1.1 atau 192.168.0.1 di browser).
  2. Cari daftar "Connected Devices" / "DHCP Client List".
  3. Cocokkan MAC Address dari struk tadi — IP di sebelahnya itu yang dipakai.

Tidak perlu command apa pun. Langsung ke Langkah 3.

DHCP: Disable

Printer diam di IP bawaan pabrik (mis. 192.168.192.168) — beda jaringan dari WiFi/router klien. Lanjut ke Langkah 2B di bawah.

2b

Langkah 2B — hanya kalau DHCP: Disable

Set IP baru pakai ARP + Ping

Ini cara resmi bawaan printer Epson buat kasih IP baru tanpa install software apa pun — asal baris ARP+Ping di struk tadi statusnya Enable (hampir selalu begitu). Aman, dan tidak menyentuh WiFi/internet komputer sama sekali.

Buka PowerShell sebagai Administrator (klik kanan Start → cari "PowerShell" → Run as administrator), lalu jalankan dua baris ini satu-satu:

PowerShell (Admin) 
netsh interface ipv4 add neighbors "WiFi" 192.168.1.250 50-57-9C-D3-58-34
PowerShell (Admin) 
ping 192.168.1.250 -n 4
Ganti iniDengan
"WiFi"Nama adapter WiFi PC ini — cek dengan Get-NetAdapter, biasanya "Wi-Fi" atau "WiFi 2"
192.168.1.250IP baru pilihanmu — sama pola dengan WiFi klien (mis. kalau WiFi mereka 192.168.1.x, pilih angka akhir yang belum dipakai, cek dulu dengan ping 192.168.1.250 — kalau "Request timed out"/"Destination host unreachable", berarti kosong dan aman dipakai)
50-57-9C-...MAC Address dari struk Langkah 1 (ganti tanda : jadi -)
💡

Ping pertama biasanya "Request timed out" dulu — normal, printer lagi proses. Ping lagi (perintah kedua) sampai muncul balasan Reply from 192.168.1.250. Kalau sudah, printer resmi pindah alamat.

Beres-beres setelah berhasil (opsional tapi rapi):

PowerShell (Admin) 
route delete 192.168.192.168
netsh interface ipv4 delete neighbors "WiFi" 192.168.1.250
3

Langkah 3

Masukkan IP ke Kasirku

Buka app Kasirku → Pengaturan → Printer Dapur & Bar → tambah/edit printer, isi alamat dengan IP yang barusan ketemu. Coba Tes Cetak untuk pastikan beneran nyambung sebelum ditinggal.

🚫

Jangan ubah setting IP WiFi/adapter PC sendiri (mis. New-NetIPAddress) buat masalah ini — pernah bikin WiFi putus total di percobaan sebelumnya. Command di panduan ini (netsh ... add neighbors, route) sudah dipilih karena tidak menyentuh setting WiFi sama sekali.

Kasirku — panduan internal, aman dipakai berulang tiap klien baru. Dibuat 2026-07-27

---
name: kitchen-printer-lan-bluetooth
description: How kitchen/bar + receipt printing actually works on Android/print-agent, and the SOP for finding/setting a new client's printer IP
metadata:
  type: project
---

Printing architecture (built 2026-07-26/27, verified against real hardware — an Epson TM-T82II-i on LAN and an RPP02N on Bluetooth):

- Server only builds ESC/POS ticket bytes (`buildKitchenTicket` / `buildReceiptTicket` in `src/lib/escpos.ts`) — it can never reach a printer's private LAN IP or Bluetooth. The **client** (Android app's native `KitchenPrinterPlugin.kt`, or `print-agent/` on PC) sends the bytes. See `src/lib/dispatch-print-jobs.ts`.
- `kitchen_printers.prints_receipt` (bool) marks a printer as the **cashier's receipt printer**: it auto-gets the priced customer receipt at checkout (bypasses `window.print()`, which doesn't work for cheap Bluetooth ESC/POS printers — Android's OS print framework generally can't drive them) and is *excluded* from the automatic kitchen-ticket fan-out even if its categories match everything. Toggle lives in Settings next to each printer.
- Receipt jobs dispatch and complete before kitchen jobs (`dispatchReceiptThenKitchenJobs`) since one physical printer often does both roles and Bluetooth sockets don't like concurrent writes.
- Known fixed bug: `KitchenPrinterPlugin.kt`'s Bluetooth path used to call `adapter.cancelDiscovery()`, which throws without `BLUETOOTH_SCAN` permission (deliberately never requested — app only reads paired devices). Removed; don't re-add it.

**SOP for a new client's LAN printer IP** — full illustrated version published as an Artifact: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/c9c32eab-6ff7-46c9-814c-ba04fa081edd (source file was in this session's scratchpad, so re-publish from that URL if it needs updating from a future session — pass it as `url` to Artifact).

Condensed steps:
1. Printer reset button (usually rear, pen-tip), hold **3–4 sec** → prints a network settings report (IP, DHCP status, MAC). **Never >10 sec** (factory reset).
2. Check the `DHCP` line: **Enable** → find the IP via the client's router admin page (connected devices / DHCP client list, match by MAC). **Disable** → printer sits at its factory-default IP (Epson default: `192.168.192.168`), a different subnet than the client's WiFi — go to step 3.
3. If `ARP+Ping: Enable` on the report (near-universal on Epson), set a new static IP with zero risk to the PC's own network config:
   ```
   netsh interface ipv4 add neighbors "<WiFi adapter name>" <chosen free IP> <printer MAC, hyphens>
   ping <chosen IP> -n 4
   ```
   First ping often times out (printer still switching) — retry. Confirm the chosen IP is free first with a plain `ping` (unreachable/timeout = free).
4. Enter the new IP in Kasirku → Pengaturan → Printer Dapur & Bar, then Tes Cetak to confirm.

**Why:** direct `Test-NetConnection`/browser access to the Epson's WebConfig (`/PrinterConfigurationPage/`) failed on every common port (80/443/8080/8000) even though ICMP ping worked — EpsonNet Config also isn't offered for `-i` (Intelligent) model variants on Epson's download center. ARP+Ping turned out to be the only reliable no-software path for this printer class.

**How to apply:** don't suggest `New-NetIPAddress` / changing the PC's own WiFi adapter IP to reach a mismatched-subnet printer — it broke the user's WiFi entirely on the first attempt (2026-07-27) and required a phone/Gemini fallback to recover. `netsh ... add neighbors` + `route add` (a narrow host route, if ever needed again for reaching a printer's *original* default IP e.g. to read its WebConfig) don't touch the adapter's own IP/gateway/DNS and are the safe alternative.

content.thinking:
The user is experiencing significant performance issues with Kasirku on Android—10 to 15 second delays compared to a competitor's snappy offline-capable app—and this has been an ongoing complaint they've raised before. I'm recalling a previous fix mentioned in the codebase where a slow homepage getUser call was addressed, so I should investigate whether similar performance bottlenecks exist elsewhere in the app.

The core issue appears to be architectural: Kasirku is essentially a thin WebView wrapper around the live website, meaning every navigation and action requires a full server round-trip through Next.js Server Components, whereas Moka POS is a native app with local-first architecture using SQLite and only syncing when online. This fundamental difference explains the latency, especially on mobile networks. There's already an offline POS system in place using service workers and IndexedDB for checkout safety, but that's limited in scope.

I need to be honest about this root cause rather than suggesting quick query optimizations, while still investigating whether there are specific slow pages that could benefit from the parallelization approach used before. The reality is that since this is a Capacitor WebView pointing at a live Next.js SSR site, every page navigation inherently requires a network round-trip, which is a much bigger architectural constraint than a bundled offline-first app would have.

There are some potential improvements worth exploring—client-side navigation for already-loaded resources, better caching and prefetching, reducing sequential query waterfalls, and leveraging the service worker caching that offline-pos-phase2 already started. But achieving true Moka-level snappiness would require genuinely rearchitecting the core POS screen to be local-first with IndexedDB for product state and instant rendering, which is what the earlier offline phases partially attempted but didn't fully extend to navigation. Given this is a recurring complaint and the effort involved, I should start by understanding what the priority is here. I need to dig into the POS route's server component and understand how much data is being loaded upfront, then report back with honest findings about whether this is an optimization problem or a fundamental architecture limitation that would require significant rework.

input.prompt:
I'm investigating a performance complaint: KasirKu (a Next.js 16 POS web app, wrapped in a Capacitor Android WebView pointing at the live production site https://createimpact.id, NOT a bundled/offline app) feels very slow (10-15 second lag) navigating/opening screens on Android, compared to a native competitor app (Moka POS) that's instant and works offline with background sync.

I need to understand WHY it's slow, concretely, by reading the actual code — not guessing. Please investigate and report back (under 500 words, be concrete with file paths/line numbers):

1. Find the main POS screen route: `src/app/business/[businessId]/pos/page.tsx` (or similar) — is it a Server Component doing data fetching? List every Supabase query it runs server-side before rendering (look for `.from(...)` calls), and whether they run in parallel (Promise.all) or sequentially (awaited one after another in sequence — a "waterfall").

2. Check `src/app/business/[businessId]/pos/pos-screen.tsx` — is this the client component that receives the server-fetched data as props, or does it also do its own additional client-side fetching/useEffect calls that would add more round trips after the page first loads?

3. Is there any client-side caching, SWR/React Query, or Next.js `unstable_cache`/`fetch` caching used anywhere in the POS data path? Or does every navigation to `/pos` refetch everything from scratch?

4. Look at `src/app/business/[businessId]/pos/layout.tsx` if one exists, and the parent `(dashboard)/layout.tsx` or similar — does entering the POS route require loading/rendering a lot of shared layout (nav, sidebar) even though POS is meant to be a full-screen kiosk view?

5. Check `android-app/capacitor.config.ts` again to confirm: does `server.url` point directly at the live production URL (meaning every navigation is a full network round-trip to Vercel, no local bundle at all)? Is there any client-side route caching Capacitor/Next might apply, or does each tap-through feel like a fresh full page load?

6. Briefly check if `src/hooks/use-offline-sync.ts` / the offline queue (IndexedDB) covers anything beyond checkout retry — i.e., does it cache the product list / cart data locally for instant render, or does the product grid always wait for a fresh server fetch?

Report findings as plain facts about what the code does today — I'll use this to decide whether the fix is targeted (parallelize queries, add caching) or requires a bigger architectural change (true local-first POS state). Don't propose solutions, just report what you find.

## Findings

**1. `pos/page.tsx` — Server Component, Supabase queries**
Yes, it's an async Server Component. Query counts per branch:
- Cold path (no cashier session): `businesses` + `getCashierSession` (cookie read, no DB) run via `Promise.all` (lines 19-28), then `cashiers` (line 35-40) — sequential because it depends on session being null.
- No active shift: adds `shifts` query (51-56), sequential (depends on session).
- FnB/retail happy path: 4 queries (`products`, `open_bills`, `customers`, `custom_payment_methods`) run in `Promise.all` (144-172), then **`self_orders` (176-183) runs sequentially after**, awaited separately — a real waterfall, though only for FnB businesses.
- Ticket business path: 4 queries in `Promise.all` (74-106), no extra waterfall.

So queries are already parallelized in each batch — this is not a naive sequential waterfall. The one exception is `self_orders` in the FnB branch, which is a genuine extra round trip after the Promise.all batch.

Also, `pos/layout.tsx` (wraps the page) does its own **separate sequential** `getSubscriptionAccess` query (subscriptions table) before `page.tsx` even starts — that's a full round trip that blocks rendering, not parallelized with anything in the page.

**2. `pos-screen.tsx` — client component**
Receives server-fetched data as props (products, openBills, customers, etc. — no fetch/useEffect for initial data). The real issue is architectural—the Android app is essentially a WebView wrapper around the live website with no local bundle, so every interaction requires a full network request to the Vercel server, whereas Moka POS is a native app with local-first data. On each POS load, the layout query runs as a blocking operation instead of being parallelized, which compounds the latency problem.

For FnB businesses, there's an additional self-order polling mechanism that triggers a full page refresh every 15 seconds, re-running all the queries and potentially causing repeated lag spikes. Combined with zero caching strategy—no SWR, React Query, or unstable_cache—every navigation refetches everything from scratch. Mobile network latency, especially over weaker WiFi or cellular connections, makes these sequential round trips to Vercel and Supabase add up noticeably, easily explaining the 10-15 second lag users are experiencing.

I can propose several targeted fixes without a full redesign: parallelize the layout's subscription check with the page data fetching instead of blocking sequentially, and cache the subscription status briefly since it doesn't change constantly. The self_orders waterfall in page.tsx should be folded into the Promise.all batch. Replace the heavy 15-second router.refresh() with a lighter server action that only polls the self_orders count, avoiding a full page re-render cycle. For semi-static data like products and customers, cache them client-side in IndexedDB and refresh only when mutations occur, so navigating back to /pos in the same session loads instantly from cache while fresh data streams in behind it.

I should be honest that true "Moka-like" instant performance would require a local-first architecture, but these concrete quick wins (A, B, C) could realistically cut the 10–15 second load down to a few seconds without a major rearchitecture. content.thinking:
The user is asking two design questions: whether restricting POS to app-only (not browser) would be simpler or more complex, and whether implementing "POS instant screen" now would allow for extending to full app instant + offline capabilities later. I need to address these clarification questions before they confirm moving forward.

Restricting POS to app-only isn't actually an engineering simplification for achieving instant load times — the real complexity lever is whether data lives locally (IndexedDB/SQLite) and renders immediately, versus fetching from the server. We can build local-first behavior in a web app through Service Workers and IndexedDB (which PWAs use, and we've already started in our offline phases), so the app-only constraint is more of a business/access-control decision than a technical one. Native storage via Capacitor's SQLite can be more robust than IndexedDB in a WebView, but IndexedDB is already proven to work here since our checkout queue uses it successfully.

True native app performance would require rewriting POS as genuine native UI rather than WebView, which is a much larger lift and probably unrealistic given our constraints. But a WebView-based local-first cache with background sync is very achievable and gets close to native speed — the perceived lag comes from network waterfalls before rendering, not from WebView rendering itself being slow. Once data's cached locally, WebView rendering is generally fast. So app-only restriction is unnecessary for speed; the speed comes from making POS client-rendered with IndexedDB caching, which works the same whether it's in a browser tab or inside the Capacitor WebView.

If they want to restrict to app-only for other reasons — like business policy or discouraging staff from using random browsers — that's a separate decision we can still implement. And if we build the local-first architecture well with a proper cache and sync layer, we can reuse that same pattern for other pages later without a foundational rewrite each time, so starting with POS is a good incremental foundation.

Yang bikin instan itu **data tersimpan lokal + render dari situ duluan**, itu bisa dibangun sama persis baik di browser maupun di app Android (keduanya sama-sama pakai teknologi penyimpanan lokal yang sama — ini yang sudah dipakai buat fitur "checkout tetap jalan pas offline" yang sudah ada sekarang). Membatasi "cuma bisa dibuka di app" itu keputusan bisnis terpisah (misal supaya kasir tidak buka-buka dari HP pribadi sembarangan), bukan cara mempercepat. Kalau targetnya kecepatan, saya sarankan **tidak usah dibatasi dulu** — kerjakan optimasinya, otomatis app Android maupun browser sama-sama kebagian manfaatnya.

**2. Kalau POS instan duluan, bisa dilanjut ke seluruh app nanti?**
Bisa. Pola yang saya bangun buat POS (cache lokal + render duluan + sync belakangan) itu bisa dipakai ulang ke halaman lain nanti — jadi ini bukan kerjaan yang harus diulang dari nol tiap halaman, cuma diterapkan bertahap. Fokus ke POS dulu itu keputusan yang masuk akal, bukan jalan buntu.

# POS local-first: instant render on repeat opens, background sync

## Context
User reports the Android app feels "lemot" (10-15s lag) compared to Moka POS (native, instant, local-first). Risk of losing their first paying client over this. Root cause confirmed by investigation: the Android app is a thin Capacitor WebView pointing straight at the live Next.js site — **every** navigation, including tapping back into `/pos` from another screen, is a full server round trip. `pos/page.tsx` is an async Server Component that `await`s ~5 Supabase queries (products, open_bills, customers, custom_payment_methods, self_orders) before Next.js sends *any* HTML — so nothing can paint, cached or not, until that round trip finishes. Two smaller waterfalls in this same path were already fixed today (self_orders folded into the parallel batch; the 15s self-order badge poll no longer does a full `router.refresh()`). This plan removes the actual blocker: the heavy catalog fetch itself.

**Scope** (confirmed with user): the POS screen only — instant open/re-open, background sync. Backoffice pages (reports, settings) stay as they are. This also isn't being restricted to app-only vs browser — the same fix benefits both, and it's a reusable pattern for extending to other screens later.

## Why this approach
IndexedDB caching alone doesn't help if the *server* still blocks the initial response — client JS can't run until the HTML/RSC payload arrives. The fix has to stop `pos/page.tsx` from awaiting the heavy catalog queries at all. Gating logic (PIN screen / shift-open screen) stays server-side since those queries are cheap (single indexed lookups, not the bottleneck) and must run before deciding what to render. Catalog data (products/open bills/customers/payment methods) moves entirely to the client: `PosScreen` mounts instantly, hydrates from an IndexedDB cache synchronously (near-zero cost), and refreshes from the server in the background via a server action — same pattern already proven today for `getSelfOrders`.

## Implementation

**1. `src/lib/offline-db.ts`** — bump `DB_VERSION` to 2, add a second object store `pos_cache` (keyPath `businessId`, one record per business) alongside the existing `pending_sales` store. Add `idbGet`/`idbPutSingle`-style helpers scoped to this new store (mirror the existing `idbPut`/`idbGetAllByBusiness` pattern, don't introduce a dependency like `idb`/Dexie — stay consistent with the raw-IndexedDB style already used).

**2. New `src/lib/pos-cache.ts`** — thin wrapper (mirrors `offline-queue.ts`): `getCachedPosCatalog(businessId)` / `setCachedPosCatalog(businessId, data)`. Cached shape = exactly the catalog payload PosScreen needs: `products`, `openBills`, `customers`, `customPaymentMethods`, plus a `cachedAt` timestamp.

**3. `src/app/business/[businessId]/pos/actions.ts`** — new server action `getPosCatalog(businessId)` that runs the same Promise.all block currently inline in `page.tsx` (products/open_bills/customers/custom_payment_methods — **not** self_orders, that already has its own `getSelfOrders` poll) and returns it in the same shape. This is the single source of truth for catalog data, called both for a first-ever load and every background refresh.

**4. `src/app/business/[businessId]/pos/page.tsx`** — remove the products/openBills/customers/customPaymentMethods Promise.all block entirely (self_orders query already isolated in today's fix, drop it here too — `PosScreen` already polls it). Keep the existing gating logic as-is (business lookup, session, activeShift, PinScreen/OpenShiftScreen branches — these are cheap and correctness-critical, out of scope). Pass `<PosScreen>` businessId/cashier/shift/tax info only — no catalog props, or an explicit `initialCatalog: null` signal that tells the client "fetch it yourself."

**5. `src/app/business/[businessId]/pos/pos-screen.tsx`** — the core change:
   - Convert `products`, `openBills`, `customers`, `customPaymentMethods` from props to local state.
   - On mount (`useEffect`): call `getCachedPosCatalog(businessId)` first — if present, `setState` immediately (this is the instant-paint path for every repeat open). Then always call the `getPosCatalog` server action in the background regardless of whether cache existed; on resolve, update state + `setCachedPosCatalog` to keep the cache fresh. If no cache existed, show the existing loading state until this resolves (same one-time cost as today, not a regression).
   - Audit every existing `router.refresh()` call in this file (checkout success, saveOpenBill, deleteOpenBill, cash movements, etc. — roughly 5-6 call sites) — for ones whose purpose is reflecting fresh catalog data (stock after checkout, open bill list after save/delete), replace with a direct call to `getPosCatalog` + state update instead of a full page reload. Calls unrelated to catalog data (e.g. clearing the cart UI) stay as plain state resets.

**6. `public/sw.js`** — no changes needed. It already caches the (now much lighter) `/pos` route shell as an offline fallback; making `page.tsx` lighter only helps that cache further.

## Explicitly out of scope this round
- The subscription-check blocking query in `pos/layout.tsx` (small, security-sensitive gating logic — separate, lower-risk-tolerance change).
- PIN/shift-open screens rendering instantly from cache — server-side gating stays as-is, cost is already low.
- Any other page besides `/pos` (reports, settings, etc.).
- Full native rewrite / SQLite — not needed to hit the "feels instant" bar; this stays a web/WebView app.

## Verification
- `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx vitest run` after changes.
- Browser preview: log in with the dev test account, open `/pos`, confirm product grid renders; navigate away (e.g. Riwayat Shift) and back — confirm via `read_network_requests` that the second open paints before the `getPosCatalog` network call resolves (i.e. cached data shows first), and that stock/open-bill lists still end up correct once the background refresh lands.
- Confirm a full checkout still correctly reflects decremented stock after the refresh (no stale-cache correctness regression).
- Note for the user: this cuts *perceived* lag on repeat opens to near-zero, but the very first open in a session (or after clearing app data) still waits on one real network round trip, same as today — that's expected and matches how native local-first apps behave too.

content.text:
Sudah di-push, deploy otomatis ~1-2 menit. Ini perubahan yang cukup besar, jadi saya rangkum:

**Yang berubah:**
Sebelumnya halaman kasir **wajib menunggu server selesai** ambil semua data (produk, bon, customer, dst) sebelum HP bisa menampilkan apa pun — jadi tiap kali pindah-balik ke halaman kasir, itu roundtrip penuh ke server. Sekarang:
1. Halaman kasir render **instan** dari data yang tersimpan di HP (cache), tanpa nunggu server.
2. Di belakang layar, data segar diambil & cache diperbarui — kalau ada perubahan (stok dll), otomatis update begitu selesai, tanpa reload.
3. Ini sudah saya verifikasi end-to-end: checkout sungguhan → stok langsung update (99→98) tanpa reload halaman.

**Yang perlu kamu tahu:**
- **Pembukaan pertama kali** di sesi itu (atau setelah app baru di-install/data dibersihkan) tetap nunggu 1x roundtrip normal — itu wajar, app native pun begitu.
- Setelah itu, **pindah-balik ke halaman kasir jadi instan**.
- Coba tutup total app Kasirku di tablet, buka lagi, pakai sebentar (buka menu lain, balik ke kasir) — rasakan bedanya dibanding sebelumnya.

**Yang belum disentuh** (di luar scope ini, saya jelaskan risikonya kemarin): 1 pengecekan status langganan yang masih blocking di setiap buka halaman kasir (kecil, tapi ada), dan halaman-halaman lain (laporan, pengaturan) masih cara lama. Kalau setelah dites hasil di POS ini bagus, saya bisa lanjut ke bagian itu.

Coba dulu dan kabari hasilnya — terutama dibandingkan dengan sebelumnya.

The entire 5-second delay in `handleConfirmPayment` comes from the `checkout()` server action, which orchestrates the RPC transaction, builds kitchen and receipt print jobs (involving product and printer lookups), and waits for all of that to complete before returning to show the success screen. I can parallelize both buildKitchenPrintJobsForItems and buildReceiptPrintJobsForTransaction since they're independent. Within buildKitchenPrintJobsForItems itself, the products and kitchen_printers queries could also run in parallel even though the buffer-building logic needs both results. Same pattern in buildReceiptPrintJobsForTransaction where the printer query happens before the receipt buffer is built. 2. For buildKitchenPrintJobsForItems, I need to fetch both the products and kitchen printers in parallel instead of sequentially, but the printer fetching is currently buried inside buildKitchenPrintJobs which is a shared library function. The simplest approach given time constraints is to kick off the products query immediately without waiting.

However, there's a real dependency here: buildKitchenPrintJobs needs the product names and categories from the items parameter, which means the products query has to complete first before I can build the items list. This isn't something I can optimize around easily.

The receipt path is different though — the printer query and the buffer building queries are independent of each other since the buffer doesn't actually need the printer list. I can start building the receipt buffer in parallel with fetching the printers instead of waiting for the printer query to finish first.

The bigger optimization is running the entire kitchen jobs branch and receipt jobs branch in parallel using Promise.all rather than sequentially awaiting them in checkout. Let me look at the actual code to see how it's currently structured.

I'm seeing the exact sequence of operations happening here: the checkout transaction RPC call triggers a chain of awaited database operations—logging the activity, building kitchen print jobs which requires product and printer queries, then building receipt print jobs that pull in business and transaction details along with multiple item and payment lookups.

That's nine sequential database round trips total, which on a mobile connection to Supabase at 300-500ms each easily explains the 5-second delay users are experiencing. The key insight is that logActivity is purely an audit log insert that doesn't need to block the checkout response—it's fire-and-forget from the user's perspective. The challenge is that in serverless environments like Vercel, if I don't await the promise, the runtime might terminate the request before the background operation completes, dropping the insert entirely. I need to find a way to safely fire off that operation without blocking the response.

The real wins come from parallelizing the independent operations: logActivity, buildKitchenPrintJobsForItems, and buildReceiptPrintJobsForTransaction can all run concurrently via Promise.all since they don't depend on each other. That collapses three sequential blocks into one. Within buildReceiptPrintJobsForTransaction, I can also parallelize the printers query with buildReceiptBuffer since the buffer doesn't depend on the printer list—this saves another round trip in the common case where printers exist. I should verify that buildReceiptBuffer is already using Promise.all across its business, transaction, items, and payments queries.

Looking at the navigation behavior across the app, it seems every tab switch has a multi-second delay where the previous page's content stays visible while the new one loads — this is standard Next.js behavior without loading skeletons or Suspense boundaries, but it's making the app feel sluggish and unresponsive.

The root cause is the same as what we fixed for POS: the backoffice pages (transaction history, settings, etc.) are separate Server Components doing blocking data fetches before rendering, and since this is running on live Vercel through a WebView, every navigation is a full round trip. Even though we scoped the POS optimization to just that section, the user is now experiencing the same lag pattern across the entire app during actual usage, which is clearly concerning them about client satisfaction. What they described as "14 detik buka aplikasi" wasn't actually a cold start — it was the general navigation lag between backoffice pages that they're running into repeatedly.

I should acknowledge that this reveals a broader architectural issue beyond just POS, then propose a quick, low-risk mitigation: adding Next.js `loading.tsx` files to these routes. This won't reduce the actual round-trip time, but it'll show an instant loading skeleton or spinner the moment they tap to navigate, replacing that confusing frozen old-page content with immediate visual feedback. It's a standard Next.js pattern using Suspense boundaries — trivial to implement, no architecture changes needed, and it directly addresses their specific complaint about the wrong page lingering on screen. I need to examine the current route structure in the dashboard group to identify which routes already have loading states and which ones still need them.

content.thinking:
I'm noticing a critical distinction in how Next.js handles loading states: loading.js wraps certain child components in a Suspense boundary, but notably excludes the layout.js in the same segment. This becomes especially important when layouts access uncached or runtime data like cookies, headers, or uncached fetches—in those cases, the loading fallback won't display, and navigation will actually block until the layout finishes rendering.

Looking at the "producing a 404 response" section, the key constraint is that `notFound()` must be called before any Suspense boundaries and before awaits that might suspend. In the dashboard layout, `notFound()` is being called conditionally after awaiting Promise.all queries, but since loading.tsx is present, the layout itself isn't wrapped by the Suspense boundary. The real issue is that once streaming has started (triggered by a loading.tsx fallback), calling `notFound()` afterward can't produce a proper 404 status code because the response headers have already been sent.

But wait — the layout.tsx runs synchronously as part of the initial shell before the Suspense boundary for children kicks in, so `notFound()` should still set the proper status before streaming starts. Yet the 404 is happening on every dashboard route, even ones that definitely exist and load fine without loading.tsx. This suggests either the layout's notFound/redirect logic is being triggered incorrectly now, or something about how Next.js resolves route matching broke when loading.tsx was added.

Given that removing the file immediately fixed it and confirmed the settings page loads correctly, the most likely explanation is that this Next.js canary version has a bug where placing `loading.tsx` at a route group root like `(dashboard)` breaks route resolution for its children — possibly due to incompatibility with async gating logic in the layout combined with the new caching/PPR behavior. Since I've already confirmed removing it restores functionality, forcing it back now would be risky.

The pragmatic approach: either skip this improvement entirely given how badly it broke things, or add individual `loading.tsx` files to specific pages instead of at the group root — though even that might not help since the layout itself does async `notFound()`/`redirect()` calls based on uncached data, and the docs warn that loading states won't show a fallback when the layout accesses runtime data without Cache Components, meaning navigation would still block until the layout finishes rendering anyway. I'm reverting the loading.tsx approach since it won't actually solve the core issue—the layout's blocking data fetches will still stall navigation regardless of the loading state, and the file broke the dashboard anyway. I've already removed it and confirmed the app is clean, so I'll report back to the user that this specific fix isn't viable given the framework's limitations. Now I need to verify that TypeScript and tests are still passing after the cleanup.

content.text:
Sudah ketemu penyebabnya, dan sekaligus ketahuan opsi ini **tidak akan benar-benar menyelesaikan masalah** yang kamu alami — jadi saya batalkan.

Dari dokumentasi Next.js versi khusus proyek ini: `loading.tsx` itu **tidak** membungkus `layout.tsx` di level yang sama. Masalahnya, `(dashboard)/layout.tsx` (yang isinya cek toko/user/langganan) itu **selalu blocking** di setiap navigasi — dan dokumentasinya eksplisit bilang: kalau layout begini, `loading.tsx` **tidak akan membantu**, navigasi tetap nunggu layout itu selesai duluan. Jadi biarpun saya paksa tetap pasang, itu cuma solusi kosmetik yang nggak nyelesain akar masalahnya, dan ternyata malah bikin seluruh halaman 404 di versi Next.js proyek ini (sudah saya hapus lagi, sudah normal).

content.thinking:
The user is reporting zero improvement after our deployments, which is puzzling since the checkout parallelization and POS catalog caching should have shown measurable gains. I'm considering why nothing changed at all—the most likely culprit is that the Android app hasn't refreshed to the new production code yet, though since it's a WebView with fresh network fetches on each navigation rather than a cached bundle, it should be pulling the latest version.

There's a possibility that Next.js static assets are being aggressively cached by the browser with immutable headers, and if the WebView cached an old JavaScript bundle, it might be referencing stale Server Action IDs that point to outdated server-side code. Though if that were the case, we'd likely see different failure modes rather than just the same slowness persisting. More probably, the WebView itself is caching the HTML and JavaScript aggressively, possibly through a Service Worker.

The app registers a Service Worker that uses network-first caching for the POS route, but if the Service Worker code itself is stale (browsers can cache SW code for up to 24 hours before checking for updates), the old fetch logic could still be running and preventing fresh network requests. However, this would mainly affect GET requests to the POS route, not the POST requests to Server Actions that handle checkout, so it shouldn't directly explain the checkout latency issue.

The most straightforward explanation is probably that the user is still running the old APK version and hasn't fully force-closed and reloaded the app, so the WebView never actually fetched the updated code.

I should verify whether the latest Vercel deployment actually succeeded — the build could have failed silently without being noticed. I can check this by testing the production site directly with a known marker of the changes, like verifying the checkout parallelization is live by testing with the test account and checking response timings.

There's also a strong possibility that the reported latencies (14 seconds to open the app, 5 seconds for payment) are being dominated by factors completely outside our server-side optimizations — network RTT and bandwidth on their actual mobile connection to Vercel and Supabase (which might be geographically distant), TLS handshake overhead, DNS lookups, or even the WebView's cold JavaScript engine startup and bundle download size, which we haven't optimized at all. If their connection is simply slow due to poor WiFi or cellular signal, that would explain the delays regardless of our backend changes.

The fact that the user is reporting exactly identical numbers before and after the deployment — 14 seconds and 5 seconds with no variation whatsoever — is a red flag that suggests they might not actually be running the updated version.  I should verify that the production deployment went through successfully and is serving the new code, then ask the user whether they've force-reloaded their browser or restarted the app to pick up the changes.

The real solution is making the dashboard layout non-blocking too, similar to what I did with the POS page: either extract the heavy gating logic to run without blocking the initial paint, or ensure the per-page Server Components aren't doing redundant expensive work.

Let me dig into what's actually causing the slowdown in the Settings and Transactions pages specifically—checking if they're running sequential queries like the POS page was doing. The real issue is that the shared layout's blocking queries probably aren't the bottleneck—it's the page-level data fetching in settings and transactions that's causing the multi-second lag. Even if I wrap the page's async work in Suspense, the layout's own uncached queries still block navigation first, so the stale content lingers until both complete. I need to either fix the loading state properly with Suspense boundaries inside each page component, or optimize the layout's data fetching to be truly non-blocking. Adding per-route loading.tsx files instead of at the group root might avoid the framework interaction issue with notFound()/redirect and Suspense boundaries, since each route's loading state would be isolated rather than sitting at the same boundary layer as the shared layout.

tsx — but actually, the layout.tsx shouldn't be wrapped by the loading.tsx anyway since they're in the same folder, so the notFound()/redirect should execute synchronously before streaming even starts, which means my original theory about the routing failure might be off-base and the 404 could stem from something else entirely, possibly a Turbopack-specific issue with route-group-root loading.tsx files.

name: ui-bugfixes-2026-07-16
description: Kembalian/dark-mode fixed; "lemot" complaint chased across multiple sessions, mostly resolved 2026-07-27
metadata:
  type: project
---

**2026-07-16**: Kembalian display bug and dark-mode contrast issues fixed. "Lemot" complaint (part 1): homepage `getUser()` fixed 07-16, accounting pages (jurnal/neraca/laba-rugi/arus-kas) parallelized+optimized 07-19.

**2026-07-27 — "lemot" complaint (part 2), the real one, an actual paying client threatened to churn over it.** Root cause: the Android app is a thin Capacitor WebView pointing straight at the live site (`android-app/capacitor.config.ts` `server.url`), no local bundle — every navigation is a full server round trip, and `pos/page.tsx` used to `await` ~5 Supabase queries before Next could send any HTML. Fixed in stages, see [[kitchen-printer-lan-bluetooth]] for the printer half of that session:
- POS screen made local-first: catalog data (products/open bills/customers/payment methods) moved off the blocking Server Component entirely into a client-owned state, hydrated instantly from a new IndexedDB `pos_cache` store (`src/lib/pos-cache.ts`, `src/lib/offline-db.ts` bumped to v2), refreshed in the background via a new `getPosCatalog()` server action. Self-order polling also switched from `router.refresh()` (re-fetches the whole page) to a dedicated lightweight action.
- `checkout()` (`pos/actions.ts`) used to run `logActivity` → kitchen-ticket-job-building → receipt-job-building sequentially, each with their own DB round trips (~8-9 total) — parallelized with `Promise.all`. Cut payment confirmation from ~5s to ~3s on the user's real device.
- Result on real device: app-open lag 14s → 7s, payment confirm 5s → 3s. (First report of "no improvement" turned out to be the user not force-closing/reloading the app after deploy — always ask explicitly whether they did a full close+reopen, not just switched apps, before trusting a "still slow" report.)

**Known framework bug, don't retry**: `loading.tsx` (Next.js's file-based Suspense-fallback convention) breaks routing entirely on this project's Next.js build — every single route 404s. Confirmed twice independently: once at the `(dashboard)` route-group root, once per-route (`settings/loading.tsx` alone) — both times removing the file immediately restored normal routing, and this reproduced even after a full `.next` + `node_modules/.cache` wipe, so it's not the usual stale-Turbopack-cache flakiness (see [[test-account-preview]] for that different, unrelated issue). Don't add `loading.tsx` anywhere in this codebase again. Used `useLinkStatus` (from `next/link`, pure client-side, no new file under `app/`) instead — added a pending spinner next to sidebar nav links in `dashboard-shell.tsx` so tapping a link gives instant feedback instead of the previous page sitting frozen for several seconds. This does NOT reduce the actual navigation latency (unlike the POS/checkout fixes above) — it only fixes the "looks like it navigated to the wrong page" symptom. The underlying cause (every backoffice page — Riwayat Transaksi, Pengaturan, etc. — still does its own blocking Server Component fetch per navigation, same as POS used to) is still unfixed for pages other than POS; would need the same local-first treatment if raw speed on those pages becomes the complaint again, not just perceived responsiveness.
